newsitem.title: GERMANY: Exhibition on German army war crimes draws crowds.
newsitem.headline: Exhibition on German army war crimes draws crowds.

text.p: Almost 90,000 people have flocked to see a German exhibition on the war crimes committed by Hitler's army which whipped up furious controversy when it opened in Munich, organisers said on Friday.

Outrage among local conservative politicians and neo-Nazis appeared to have pulled in visitors to the exhibition, which had previously drawn only 130,000 viewers in total in 16 other German and Austrian cities.
A spokesman for Munich's city council said an average of 2,000 people had come each day, many of them prepared to queue for hours to get in.
Munich had special significance for Hitler's Nazis, who awarded it the title "Capital City of the Movement".

The exhibition uses photographs and letters from soldiers themselves to back up its premise that the regular army, the Wehrmacht, as well as the SS units usually blamed for war crimes, participated in mass killings of Jews and other atrocities.

Bavaria's arch-conservative Christian Social Union, partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition, found themselves lined up with local neo-Nazi groups in opposition to the exhibition, while left-wing groups turned out in counter-protests.

The controversy prompted a debate in the Bonn parliament, where some deputies broke down crying at the speaker's podium as they told harrowing tales of their families' sufferings and gave embarrassing details of rabid Nazis among their relatives.

The exhibition is organised by a research foundation set up by billionaire philanthropist and art patron Jan Philipp Reemstma. It closes this weekend to move to Frankfurt, and will continue to show in various cities until the end of 1999.
